name: Eventbrite
description: Eventbrite orders and check-ins become events for the events you choose: Placed Order (orders paid through a payment processor, once, in their currency), Registered for Event (free and other orders, no value), Refunded Order (once per refund Eventbrite has processed, its own amount) and Checked In. Eventbrite's webhooks only point at the order or attendee, so DumbMail fetches each one with your Eventbrite token. Buyers and attendees are held back from marketing: a ticket isn't consent.

credentials.name: token
credentials.label: Eventbrite private token
credentials.help: Eventbrite → Account settings → Developer links → API keys → your key's private token. Used to fetch each order and attendee a webhook points to.

setup: Create the integration from this recipe and copy its webhook URL. Keep it private: Eventbrite doesn't sign webhooks, so the URL is the secret (Eventbrite's docs say the same).
In Eventbrite, open Account settings → Developer links → API keys and copy your private token. Save it as the credential token.

Set event_ids in the integration's settings to the IDs of the events to record (the number in each event's address), for example ["123456789"]. Orders and check-ins for other events are ignored, whatever a webhook says.

Still in Account settings → Developer links, open Webhooks → Add webhook. Paste the webhook URL, pick the event (or All events), tick Order placed, Order updated, Order refunded and Attendee checked in, and save. Click Test to send a test delivery.
Place a test order and check the delivery log: each webhook is followed by a fetch of the order with its refund request.

Placed Order is recorded only for an order Eventbrite shows as placed with a payment processor fee (paid through a payment processor); free orders and orders paid some other way are Registered for Event, with no value. A refund counts once Eventbrite marks it processed, for the amount it processed.
DumbMail looks up at most 1,000 records an hour for this integration (Eventbrite allows 2,000 calls an hour per token); past that, webhooks wait and are tried again.

Buyers and attendees are held back from marketing: buying a ticket isn't consent. Eventbrite's own opt-in preferences (contact_list_preferences) aren't read. Flows marked as service messages (an order follow-up, say) still reach them.
Barcodes, answers to custom questions and addresses are never stored: only the fields the recipe reads are kept.
